q8.answer: Each customer's count lives in one shared Redis primary (with a replica for failover), so all six gateway instances read and write the same key, rl/<customerId>/<windowStart>. Old counts are removed by a TTL: the key expires 61 seconds after its first increment.

q9.answer: The budget resets at each whole minute. The window key includes windowStart, so a new minute starts a fresh counter at zero, and the previous minute's key expires on its own after 61 seconds. A customer can therefore send up to about twice the limit across a minute boundary, which is accepted for v1.

q10.answer: The check and the increment run together in one Lua script, and Redis runs a script as a single uninterrupted step with no other command interleaved. Two instances therefore cannot both take the last free slot, and the script only increments when the count is under the limit, so a 429 never uses budget.

q11.answer: Redis computes it inside the script from its own clock (TIME) as window - (now % window), which is the number of seconds until the current one-minute window ends. The result is always a whole number from 1 to 60 and is returned with the script's allowed/denied result.

q12.answer: No. The 50 ms deadline covers the whole store call and there is no retry. The gateway forwards the request, emits ratelimit_store_unavailable, and omits the X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers, so the client gets no rate-limit information for that response. A timeout may still have applied the increment, which the design accepts.
